_comment: International (INN) and common everyday drug-name aliases -> RxNorm (USAN) names.
WHY: RxNorm is a US vocabulary. It knows 'acetaminophen' and has never heard of
'paracetamol', the name most of the world uses. Without these, a user outside the US
types the only name they know, sees an empty list, and reasonably concludes the app
does not know their medication.
SAFETY RULES — every entry must satisfy all three:
1. The target must exist verbatim in drugs.json (tools/validate-synonyms.mjs
enforces this; a broken alias is dead weight).
2. The alias and target must be THE SAME DRUG. An alias is a naming difference,
never a substitution. 'gliclazide' -> 'glipizide' was rejected for exactly this
reason: gliclazide is absent from RxNorm (not US-approved) and glipizide is a
DIFFERENT sulfonylurea. Silently redirecting someone to another medication is
far worse than showing them nothing and letting them type it as free text.
3. No guessing. Drugs absent from RxNorm (domperidone, gliclazide, oral rehydration
salts) are simply omitted. Free-text entry already covers them.
Ambiguous mappings are also omitted: 'vitamin b12' could mean hydroxocobalamin or
mecobalamin, and picking one for the user would be inventing information.
Aliases are additive — they add a searchable name pointing at an existing concept.
They never create a drug and never touch disease links, so they cannot change what
the app claims a drug treats.
